item.research_question: How can a catalyst be designed to simultaneously achieve high methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) mass activity and strong resistance to CO poisoning, overcoming the trade-off between needing contiguous Pt atoms for activity and isolated Pt atoms to prevent poisoning?
item.material_system: High-entropy alloyed single-atom Pt (HEASA-Pt) with composition Pt1-NiCoMgBiSn (2.3 at% Pt, Co, Ni, Sn, Bi, Mg) supported on carbon nanotube (CNT) films; compared against HEA-Pt (Pt content >5 at%) and commercial Pt/C.
item.processing_route: In-situ Joule-heating method: Metal chloride precursors dip-coated on super-aligned CNT films were rapidly heated to ~1100 °C for 3 s in 10% H2/90% Ar atmosphere, followed by natural cooling at rates >1000 °C/s.
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical measurements in 1 M KOH + 1 M methanol (three-electrode system, Hg/HgO reference, Pt counter); Chronoamperometry (CA) at 0.7 V vs. RHE for up to 180,000 s; DMFC tests at 80 °C with 6.0 M KOH electrolyte and 1 M CH3OH fuel; In-situ FTIR from -0.7 to 0.5 V vs. Hg/HgO.
key_findings: HEASA-Pt (2.3 at% Pt) achieved a mass activity of 35.3 A mg−1, significantly outperforming commercial Pt/C (1.56 A mg−1) and HEA-Pt (3.65–17.6 A mg−1).
The catalyst maintained high activity after 180,000 s of operation, retaining 94.7% of current density and 83.4% of CV peak current after nine 20,000 s cycles with electrolyte refreshment.
In-situ FTIR spectroscopy showed no CO adsorption peak (1950–2100 cm−1) for HEASA-Pt, indicating a CO-free reaction pathway, whereas HEA-Pt showed a distinct *CO signal at 2049 cm−1.
DFT calculations revealed that CO adsorption on HEASA-Pt was weakened by more than 0.7 eV compared to Pt(111), reducing the energy barrier for *CO oxidation to 0.50 eV.
The HCOOH pathway on HEASA-Pt had a free-energy change of 0.52 eV, compared to 0.93 eV on Pt(111), facilitating an alternative route that bypasses CO formation.
DMFCs equipped with HEASA-Pt anodes reached a peak power density of 22.8 mW cm−2 with only 0.08 mg cm−2 Pt, compared to 17.2 mW cm−2 for Pt/C anodes with 0.4 mg cm−2 Pt.
XPS analysis confirmed Pt exists in a more negative valence state in HEASA-Pt than in Pt/C, consistent with electron donation from main-group elements (Mg, Bi, Sn).
Pt-free HEA (BiMgSnCoNi) exhibited no MOR activity, confirming Pt is the essential active site within the high-entropy matrix.
item.mechanism: The high-entropy structure induces a synergistic effect where multiple alloying elements (Co, Ni, Sn, Bi, Mg) coordinate around isolated Pt atoms. This coordination modifies the electronic structure (lowering the d-band center) to weaken *CO adsorption and facilitates the oxidation of *CO via adjacent oxophilic elements (e.g., Co) acting as OH donors. Simultaneously, the isolated nature of Pt sites prevents the formation of contiguous Pt ensembles required for the CO pathway, forcing the reaction through a CO-free HCOOH pathway.
item.limitations: The text notes that when Pt content exceeds 5 at%, contiguous Pt atoms form, leading to CO poisoning; it also mentions that high Bi content can aggregate and block Pt sites, requiring moderate Bi content. Additionally, long-term CA testing showed activity loss due to carbonate/bicarbonate precipitation, though this was reversible.
item.future_work: The authors propose that this work demonstrates a universal high-entropy alloyed single-atom strategy to address CO poisoning, beneficial for achieving high-efficiency DMFCs at low cost, implying future applications in similar catalytic systems.
quotes: This catalyst not only possesses active Pt sites but also inherits the ability of single-atom Pt to resist CO poisoning.
The high-entropy structure induces a synergistic effect, wherein the elements coordinated around single-atom Pt sites effectively remove adsorbed CO from Pt.

HEASA-Pt2.3% has the highest mass activity, 35.3 A mg–1, outperforming commercial Pt/C catalyst (1.56 A mg1), SA-Pt@C (almost no catalytic activity), and HEA-Pt with higher Pt contents (3.65–17.6 A mg−1).
